title: Leg pain and a foot ulcer in a 75-year-old man with diabetes: peripheral vascular examination
desc: This station involves a focused history and peripheral vascular examination of the lower limbs in Daniel Clayton, a 75-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol and a heavy smoking history, who comes to his GP with left leg pain. In Part 2 the candidate interprets a wound assessment with a photograph, the ankle-brachial index and toe pressures, and blood results. They describe and diagnose an arterial ulcer with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, then outline urgent vascular referral, wound care without elevation or compression, risk factor modification and safety netting.
focus: Peripheral vascular examination of the lower limbs, then describing an arterial ulcer, interpreting the ABI and arranging management
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a general practice. Mr Daniel Clayton, a 75-year-old retired carpenter, has come in with pain in his left leg. He has long-standing type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol, for which he takes metformin and atorvastatin. Your GP supervisor has asked you to see him first. The practice nurse is available and the practice has a handheld Doppler.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Clayton and perform a peripheral vascular examination of his lower limbs, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the practice nurse's wound assessment and photograph of the ulcer, his ankle-brachial index and toe pressures, and his blood and urine results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Daniel Clayton, a 75-year-old retired carpenter. You are a bit worn out from poor sleep and your left foot hurts. You are friendly and matter-of-fact. Lie on the bed in your shorts when asked; the candidate should expose your legs to above the knees (to the groin, keeping your underwear on). The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "It's my left leg, doc. It's been playing up for a while, and now I've got a sore on my foot that just won't heal."

History (give only when asked):

  • Pain on walking: for about a year you have had a cramping ache in your left calf when you walk. A year ago it came on after about 400 m; now it comes on after about 100 m, "barely to the end of the street". It goes away within 2 or 3 minutes of standing still. It comes on at the same distance every time, and faster going uphill. No pain in the buttocks or thighs. Your right calf aches a little on long walks, but much less.
  • Pain at night: for about the last month your left foot aches at night, mostly in the toes and front of the foot, and wakes you up. It eases if you hang your foot over the side of the bed or get up and walk around the room. A few nights you have slept in the recliner. Raising the leg on a pillow makes it worse.
  • The sore: you noticed it about 6 weeks ago on the inner side of your left big toe joint, where your new work boots rubbed. It has not got any smaller. It is painful (about 6 out of 10, worse at night and when your leg is up). Very little comes out of it. You have been putting a plaster on it.
  • Infection (only if asked): no fever or shivers, no spreading redness, swelling, pus or bad smell, no black skin.
  • Sudden change (only if asked): nothing sudden. The foot has never suddenly gone cold, white, blue or numb, and you can move your toes normally.
  • Other causes (only if asked): no back pain, and the leg pain does not come on from just standing; bending forward or sitting does not help more than standing still. No numbness, pins and needles or burning in your feet. No leg swelling, varicose veins or clots in the legs.
  • Heart and circulation: no chest pain or tightness, no stroke or mini-stroke, no sudden loss of vision or weakness. A smoker's cough in the mornings; a little puffed on hills, but the calf stops you first.
  • Diabetes: type 2 for about 20 years. Metformin 1 g twice a day. The GP said your last sugar test was "a bit high". You don't check your feet and have never seen a podiatrist. Your eyes were last checked about 2 years ago ("some early changes").
  • Other medical history: high cholesterol. A doctor once said your blood pressure was "borderline"; you take nothing for it. No kidney problems.
  • Medicines: metformin 1 g twice a day and atorvastatin 20 mg at night. No aspirin or other blood thinner. No steroids (tablets, injections or creams). Paracetamol now and then. Allergies: none.
  • Smoking: you started at 18 and smoked about 15 a day for most of your life; you cut down to about 10 a day a few years ago (about 40 pack-years). You have tried to quit twice on your own.
  • Alcohol: about 2 beers most nights.
  • Family history: your father died of a stroke at 70. Your brother has diabetes.
  • Social: you live with your wife, Margaret, in your own home and you still drive. You used to walk the dog every day and potter in your shed, but now you can't walk far.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you thought it was "just old age" and the new boots. You are frightened because a mate from the bowls club with diabetes had his leg taken off last year. You were hoping for a cream for the sore and something to help you sleep.

Question to raise (near the end of Part 1, if not already covered): "It's just a bit of poor circulation, isn't it?"

Use plain language and say you don't follow if the candidate uses jargon.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: overweight older man, comfortable at rest, in mild discomfort when his left foot is raised. No walking aids. Walks slowly with a normal gait. Wearing tight leather work boots with no inserts; the inside of the left boot is worn over the big toe joint.
  • Vital signs: BP 140/85 mmHg, HR 76 beats/min regular, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C (afebrile), RR 16/min. Bedside glucose (if asked): 11.2 mmol/L.
  • Inspection of the legs: left shin and foot shiny and hairless, with thickened, yellow toenails; the right leg shows sparse hair only. Left calf visibly thinner than the right. Left foot pale when lying flat. No amputations, gangrene or necrosis, no venous staining, varicose veins or lipodermatosclerosis, no scars, no Charcot deformity. Heels, soles and between the toes: intact skin, no callus, no fissures, no other ulcers. An ulcer is present on the medial side of the left first metatarsophalangeal joint. If the candidate starts to describe it, say: "You will be shown a photograph and the wound assessment in Part 2."
  • Temperature (back of the hand): both legs warm to the knee; the left foot and lower shin are cooler than the right.
  • Capillary refill (big toe): left 5 seconds, right 3 seconds.
  • Venous filling: left foot veins refill slowly (about 25 seconds); right normal.
  • Oedema: no pitting oedema.
  • Pulses: femoral pulses present both sides, left weaker than right, with a soft bruit over the left femoral artery. Popliteal: right present, left not felt. Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis: right present but weak, left not felt. Abdominal aorta: not expansile, no bruit.
  • Buerger's test: left leg goes pale on elevation to about 20 degrees (Buerger's angle 20 degrees); when hung over the side of the bed it slowly turns a dusky red-purple. Right leg keeps its colour at 45 degrees.
  • Ankle-brachial index: if the candidate says they would measure it, ask: "How would you do that?" The result is given in Part 2.
  • Sensation: 10 g monofilament felt at all four sites on both feet (pulp of the big toe and the first, third and fifth metatarsal heads). Vibration (128 Hz fork at the big toe), proprioception, sharp touch and temperature: normal in both feet.
  • Other (if mentioned): urine dipstick glucose 2+, protein trace, otherwise negative. Fundoscopy: scattered dot haemorrhages and microaneurysms in both eyes. Cardiovascular examination: regular pulse, normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no carotid bruits. Chest clear.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self (name and role), confirms Mr Clayton's identity, explains the examination and gains consent.
Positions him lying on the bed and exposes both legs to at least above the knees (to the groin with underwear on), maintaining his dignity.
Uses plain language, is gentle with the painful foot, acknowledges his fear of losing his leg, and answers his question that this is more than poor circulation.
History
Characterises the leg pain:

kids.x: Claudication: site (left calf), cramping pain on walking that comes on at a set distance (now about 100 m, was 400 m) and goes within minutes of rest.
Rest pain: night pain in the left forefoot that wakes him and eases when the foot hangs down, worse with elevation.
kids.d: Credit only if the candidate asks about pain at night or at rest.

kids.x: Asks about a sudden change: foot suddenly cold, pale, blue, numb or weak (acute limb ischaemia).
Asks about features of other causes: back pain or pain on standing relieved by bending forward (spinal stenosis), numbness or burning (neuropathy), leg swelling or varicose veins (venous disease).

check.x: Explores the ulcer: when and how it started (boot rubbing 6 weeks ago), not healing, pain, discharge, and signs of infection (fever, spreading redness, pus, smell, black skin).
check.d: Infection screening is the critical element.

check.x: Takes the vascular risk factors:

kids.x: Diabetes: type, duration, control, complications (eyes, kidneys, nerves) and foot care or podiatry.
Smoking quantified (about 40 pack-years, still smoking 10 a day) and attempts to quit.
BP, cholesterol, family history (father's stroke at 70), and other vascular disease: angina, stroke or TIA.

check.x: Takes medicines (metformin, atorvastatin 20 mg, no antiplatelet, no steroids) and allergies (none).
check.d: Asking about steroids or other medicines that slow healing is extra credit; the item is earned for the current medicines, antiplatelet status and allergies.

check.x: Asks about function and social history: walking distance, daily function and home support.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thought it was old age and the boots, fears amputation like his friend, wants a cream and better sleep.
Examination
General inspection: well or unwell, pain or distress, walking aids, gait, body habitus, and looks at his shoes for fit, wear and inserts.
Asks for the vital signs: blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation and temperature.
Inspects the whole of both lower limbs:

kids.x: Trophic changes: hair loss, shiny skin, nail changes, muscle wasting, colour (pallor, erythema).
Looks at the heels, soles and between the toes for ulcers, necrosis or gangrene, and notes amputations and scars.
Looks for venous signs (staining, varicosities) and Charcot joints.

check.x: Palpates for perfusion:

kids.x: Temperature with the back of the hand from thigh to foot, comparing sides (left foot cooler).
Capillary refill at the big toe (left 5 seconds, right 3 seconds; normal 2 seconds or less).
Venous filling (slow on the left).
Pitting oedema (none).

check.x: Palpates the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses on both sides, comparing strength, and palpates the abdominal aorta (finds absent left popliteal and pedal pulses).
check.d: All four levels on both sides and the aorta are needed.

check.x: Performs Buerger's test correctly (elevates the leg to 45 degrees watching for pallor, then hangs it over the bed at 90 degrees watching for rubor or cyanosis) and reports a positive test on the left.

When asked, explains the ankle-brachial index: after 10 minutes lying flat, measures the brachial systolic pressure in both arms and the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial systolic pressures with the cuff just above the ankle and a handheld Doppler, then divides the higher of the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressure by the higher brachial pressure; an ABI of 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease.
check.d: Credit for: rest supine, brachial pressures in both arms, ankle pressures with Doppler, higher ankle divided by higher brachial, and 0.90 or below = PAD. Exact rest time not required.

check.x: Tests for loss of protective sensation in both feet with a 10 g monofilament (three sites: hallux and first and fifth metatarsal heads, or four sites including the third metatarsal head) and/or vibration with a 128 Hz tuning fork at the big toe.
check.d: Monofilament or 128 Hz vibration (or the Ipswich touch test if neither is available) earns the item; proprioception, sharp touch or temperature alone does not.

check.x: States they would complete the examination with a urine dipstick (glucose), fundoscopy and a cardiovascular examination.
Interpretation
Describes the ulcer from the photograph and wound assessment:
check.d: Credit in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer.

kids.x: Site: over a non-weight-bearing bony prominence (medial left first metatarsophalangeal joint).
Size and edge: 2 cm x 2 cm, about 4 mm deep with no tendon or bone exposed, well circumscribed, symmetrical and punched out.
kids.d: Credit "deep" or "steep punched-out walls"; do not penalise "superficial" from a diabetic foot classification.

kids.x: Base: pale and white with very little granulation and minimal exudate.
Surrounding skin: no cellulitis or other sign of infection; probe to bone negative.
kids.d: Must state there are no signs of infection (no cellulitis, probe to bone negative); credit also if stated in the differentials answer.

check.x: Calculates and interprets the ABI and toe pressures: ABI left 0.56 (80/142) and right 0.79 (112/142) (0.90 or below = bilateral PAD, worse on the left), and a left toe pressure of 24 mmHg (below 30) = severe ischaemia with poor healing potential without revascularisation.
check.d: Noting monophasic waveforms or that diabetes can falsely raise the ABI is good practice but not required.

check.x: Interprets the bloods: HbA1c 8.6% above target, LDL 2.6 mmol/L above the target for vascular disease, normal WCC and CRP (no sign of infection), eGFR 64 and a raised urine albumin to creatinine ratio (possible diabetic kidney disease; relevant to contrast).
States the diagnosis: arterial (ischaemic) ulcer of the left foot from peripheral arterial disease, with rest pain and tissue loss meaning chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
check.d: Credit 'arterial ulcer with critical limb ischaemia'. Also credit ischaemic diabetes-related foot ulcer with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.

check.x: Gives at least two differentials, each with a feature for or against (neuropathic ulcer, venous ulcer, infected ulcer or osteomyelitis, spinal stenosis, acute limb ischaemia).
Management

Refers urgently to vascular surgery (seen within days) for an arterial duplex ultrasound of the lower limb and assessment for revascularisation: balloon angioplasty or surgical bypass, with amputation only in severe cases.
check.d: Routine outpatient referral or 'review in a few months' does not earn this item.

check.x: Advises rest without elevating the leg and states that compression must not be used, explaining that both reduce blood flow to the foot and may worsen the ulcer.
Wound care: a suitable dressing, offloading by stopping the tight boots, and no antibiotics or swab as the ulcer is not infected.
Starts secondary prevention for symptomatic peripheral arterial disease:

kids.x: Antiplatelet: aspirin 100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg daily.
High-intensity statin: increase atorvastatin to 40 to 80 mg, aiming for LDL below 1.8 mmol/L.

check.x: Advises stopping smoking completely as the single most important change, offers support (Quitline 13 78 48) and pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement or varenicline).
Plans to intensify diabetes treatment and to recheck BP and the uACR (ACE inhibitor or ARB if BP stays above 130/80 or albuminuria is confirmed).
check.d: Credit intensifying diabetes treatment plus either BP or uACR follow-up; HbA1c target and thresholds are extra credit. Avoiding a new SGLT2 inhibitor while the ischaemic ulcer is active and continuing metformin at eGFR 64 are also extra credit, not required.

check.x: Offers analgesia for rest pain (regular paracetamol, short-term opioid if needed).
check.d: Reviewing medicines that slow healing, such as steroids (he takes none), is extra credit.

check.x: Explains to Mr Clayton in plain words that the arteries to his leg are narrowed, why the sore is not healing, why he should not raise his leg, and answers honestly about amputation (the aim of urgent treatment is to save the leg).
Safety netting
Tells him to call 000 or go to ED straight away if the foot suddenly becomes very painful, cold, white or blue, numb or weak.
Tells him to be seen the same day (GP or ED) for signs of infection or gangrene: spreading redness, swelling, pus, a bad smell, black skin, fever or feeling unwell.
Arranges follow-up: practice nurse wound review at least weekly, podiatry or high-risk foot service, and GP review in 1 to 2 weeks for medicines, smoking and diabetes.

part2.lead: Here is the practice nurse's wound assessment with a photograph of the ulcer, the ankle-brachial index and toe pressures she measured today, and his blood and urine results from samples taken last week when he booked this appointment.
part2.patient:
Mr Clayton stays for the explanation. When the candidate explains the plan or answers the fourth question, he asks, if not already covered:

  • "My wife says I should keep my leg up on a pillow to help the sore heal. Should I?"
  • "Am I going to lose my leg like my mate did?"
  • "I've cut down to ten a day. Isn't that enough?"

He is relieved by an honest, clear answer and agrees to see the vascular surgeon and to try to quit.

handover.label: Wound assessment and photograph of the left foot ulcer
handover.result:
Practice nurse wound assessment, today. Photograph attached (medial view of the left foot).

  • Site: medial aspect of the left first metatarsophalangeal joint, over the bony prominence. Not on the sole.
  • Size: 2.0 cm x 2.0 cm, depth about 0.4 cm. No tendon or bone visible. Probe to bone: negative.
  • Edge: round, sharply defined and regular, with steep 'punched-out' walls.
  • Base: pale, whitish tissue with very little granulation tissue; no slough or eschar.
  • Exudate: minimal, serous. No odour.
  • Surrounding skin: pale, thin and hairless. No erythema, warmth, swelling or induration. No callus. No undermining.
  • Pain: 6/10, worse at night and on elevation.
  • Duration: about 6 weeks, no change in size.
handover.model:
Read: a small (2 x 2 cm) ulcer, about 4 mm deep with steep punched-out walls and no tendon or bone exposed, well circumscribed and symmetrical, on a non-weight-bearing bony prominence of the left foot, with a pale, poorly granulating base, minimal exudate and no surrounding cellulitis. Probe to bone is negative. (By a diabetic foot classification such as University of Texas or SINBAD it is superficial, as it does not reach tendon, capsule or bone; accept either description.)

For Mr Clayton: these are the features of an arterial ulcer: site at a pressure point from his boot, punched-out edge, pale base, little exudate and a lot of pain. It is not a neuropathic ulcer (not plantar, no callus, painful, intact monofilament) or a venous ulcer (not in the gaiter area, small, deep, dry, no venous skin changes). There are no clinical signs of infection.

What it changes: it will not heal without better blood supply. No antibiotics or wound swab for an uninfected ulcer. Offload (stop the boots), dress it, and refer to vascular surgery.

handover.label: Ankle-brachial index and toe pressures (handheld Doppler, today)
handover.result:
Ankle-brachial index and toe pressures, performed by the practice nurse after 10 minutes supine rest. Handheld Doppler and cuff; toe pressures by photoplethysmography.

SiteRight (mmHg)Left (mmHg)
Brachial systolic142138
Dorsalis pedis systolic11280
Posterior tibial systolic10674
Hallux (toe) systolic6224

Doppler waveforms: right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial biphasic; left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial monophasic and damped.
handover.model:
Read: using the higher brachial pressure (142 mmHg), the right ABI is 0.79 and the left 0.56. An ABI of 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease, so there is disease in both legs, mild on the right and moderate on the left. Left pedal waveforms are monophasic. The toe-brachial index is abnormal on both sides (right 0.44, left 0.17; 0.75 or above makes PAD less likely per the Australian guideline), and the left toe pressure is 24 mmHg.

For Mr Clayton: in diabetes the ankle arteries may be calcified and hard to compress, so the ABI can be falsely normal or high; toe pressures are more reliable. A toe pressure below 30 mmHg means severe ischaemia and a low chance of the ulcer healing. With rest pain and an ulcer, this is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.

What it changes: the Australian diabetes-related foot disease guideline calls for urgent vascular imaging and consideration of revascularisation when toe pressure is below 30 mmHg. Compression is not used.

handover.label: Blood and urine results (collected last week)
handover.result: Non-fasting sample collected last week, 09:15. Taking metformin 1 g twice daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.
handover.model:
Read: HbA1c 8.6% (70 mmol/mol) and random glucose 11.4 mmol/L: poorly controlled diabetes. LDL 2.6 mmol/L on atorvastatin 20 mg, above the target of below 1.8 for established vascular disease, with low HDL and raised triglycerides. Normal Hb, WCC and CRP. Creatinine 98 with eGFR 64 and a raised urine albumin to creatinine ratio of 4.8 mg/mmol.

For Mr Clayton: uncontrolled risk factors are driving his arterial disease and slowing healing. A normal WCC and CRP fit an uninfected ulcer. The albuminuria suggests diabetic kidney disease (confirm on repeat), and his kidney function matters for contrast angiography and for metformin dosing (no change needed at eGFR 64).

What it changes: increase to a high-intensity statin, start an antiplatelet, intensify diabetes treatment, and repeat the urine albumin to creatinine ratio.

rows.n: Target for most adults with type 2 diabetes 7.0% or below
Confirm with 2 of 3 samples over 3 to 6 months

ask: You are now calling the vascular surgery registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Clayton, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Clayton now, here in general practice.
Before Mr Clayton goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student at the practice for Dr [GP]. Daniel Clayton, 75.
  • Situation: non-healing painful left foot ulcer for 6 weeks with night rest pain: suspected chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. Requesting urgent vascular review.
  • Background: type 2 diabetes 20 years on metformin, high cholesterol on atorvastatin 20 mg, smokes 10 a day (40 pack-years), left calf claudication now 100 m. No antiplatelet, no allergies.
  • Assessment: absent left popliteal and pedal pulses, weaker left femoral pulse with bruit, suggesting multilevel disease including inflow; cool left foot, CRT 5 s, Buerger's angle 20 degrees, sensation intact. Ulcer 2 x 2 cm over medial left first MTP joint: punched out, pale base, minimal exudate, no cellulitis, probe to bone negative. ABI L 0.56, R 0.79 with monophasic left pedal waveforms; left toe pressure 24 mmHg (below 30, severe ischaemia; toe pressures more reliable than ABI in diabetes). HbA1c 8.6% and LDL 2.6 (both above target), WCC and CRP normal (no infection), eGFR 64 with uACR 4.8 (likely diabetic kidney disease, relevant to contrast).
  • Recommendation: urgent clinic review and arterial duplex for revascularisation planning; starting antiplatelet and high-intensity statin.

Most likely: arterial ulcer from peripheral arterial disease, with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (rest pain and tissue loss). For it: worsening claudication, rest pain eased by hanging the foot down, punched-out pale ulcer on a bony prominence, absent left pulses, positive Buerger's, ABI 0.56 and toe pressure 24 mmHg.

  • Neuropathic ulcer: long-standing diabetes. Against: painful, not plantar, no callus, intact monofilament.
  • Venous ulcer: against: not in the gaiter area, small, deep and dry, no venous skin changes or oedema.
  • Infected ulcer or osteomyelitis (must exclude): diabetic, 6-week ulcer over a bony prominence. Against: no cellulitis, afebrile, probe to bone negative, normal WCC and CRP.
  • Acute limb ischaemia: against: gradual, no sudden cold, numb or weak foot.
  • Spinal stenosis: against: no back pain, relief on standing still.

1. Urgent vascular surgery referral (seen within days): arterial duplex ultrasound, then angioplasty or bypass; amputation only if severe.
  2. Rest; do not elevate the leg and no compression: both reduce blood flow.
  3. Wound: a suitable dressing; offload by stopping the tight boots; no antibiotics or swab (not infected).
  4. Antiplatelet: aspirin 100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg daily. Statin: atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg (LDL below 1.8).
  5. Stop smoking: Quitline 13 78 48, nicotine replacement or varenicline.
  6. Diabetes and BP: intensify diabetes treatment; recheck BP and repeat the uACR (ACE inhibitor or ARB if BP stays above 130/80 or albuminuria is confirmed). Extra credit: HbA1c target about 7%.
  7. Pain: regular paracetamol, short-term opioid if needed for rest pain. Extra credit: review medicines that slow healing (steroids: none).

• Plain words: narrowed arteries mean the sore is not getting enough blood to heal; keep the leg down, not up; urgent treatment aims to save the leg; stopping smoking completely matters most.
  • Call 000 or go to ED if the foot suddenly becomes very painful, cold, white or blue, numb or weak.
  • Same day GP or ED for spreading redness, swelling, pus, a bad smell, black skin, fever or feeling unwell.
  • Follow-up: practice nurse wound review at least weekly; podiatry or high-risk foot service; GP review in 1 to 2 weeks for medicines, smoking and diabetes; arrange retinal screening (overdue, background retinopathy); check his feet daily.

ddx.dx: Arterial (ischaemic) ulcer from peripheral arterial disease with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
ddx.for: Worsening left calf claudication, night rest pain eased by hanging the foot down, a punched-out pale ulcer on a bony prominence, absent left popliteal and pedal pulses, Buerger's angle 20 degrees, ABI 0.56 and toe pressure 24 mmHg in a smoker with diabetes.
Twenty years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.6% and an ulcer from footwear pressure.
ddx.against: The ulcer is painful, not on the sole, has no callus, and monofilament and vibration sensation are intact.

ddx.for: Chronic non-healing ulcer in an older man.
ddx.against: Not in the gaiter area, small, deep and dry, with no venous staining, varicose veins or oedema.

ddx.for: Leg pain on walking in a 75-year-old.
ddx.against: No back pain, pain eases on standing still rather than bending forward, and the pulses and ABI are abnormal.

ddx.dx: Infected diabetes-related foot ulcer or osteomyelitis
ddx.for: 6-week ulcer over a bony prominence in a man with diabetes.
ddx.against: No cellulitis, pus or odour, afebrile, probe to bone negative, and normal WCC and CRP.

ddx.for: Pale, cool left foot with absent pedal pulses.
ddx.against: Gradual worsening over a year, no sudden pain, coldness, numbness or weakness, and sensation and movement are normal.

guide:
Part 1: allow about 4 minutes for the history, then prompt "please move on to the examination" if needed. Give findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. When the candidate finds the ulcer, tell them it will be shown in Part 2; its description is marked in Part 2 (item 23), not in Part 1. If the candidate mentions the ABI, ask "How would you do that?" and mark item 19 on the explanation; the numbers come in Part 2. For sensation, a monofilament or 128 Hz vibration (or the Ipswich touch test if neither is available) earns item 20; proprioception, sharp touch or temperature alone does not. For the monofilament, accept three or four sites.

Part 2: hand over all three results together (show the photograph if you have one) and ask the four questions in order. Credit the ulcer description and result interpretation in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. Mr Clayton asks his questions during the management or safety-netting answers if the candidate has not covered them.

A high-performing candidate asks about rest pain and sudden change, quantifies smoking, examines all pulse levels and the feet including between the toes, performs Buerger's test, explains the ABI and tests sensation. In Part 2 they describe the ulcer systematically, recognise that toe pressures matter in diabetes, name chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, refer urgently to vascular surgery and clearly advise against elevation and compression.

A borderline candidate misses the rest pain, palpates only the foot pulses, calls it a neuropathic or venous ulcer, applies compression or advises elevation, starts antibiotics for an uninfected ulcer, or makes a routine referral.
explain:
The diagnosis: arterial ulcer with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia

Mr Clayton has a year of worsening left calf claudication, a month of night rest pain eased by hanging the foot down, and a 6-week painful ulcer that started where his boot rubbed. He has absent left popliteal and pedal pulses, a cool pale foot with slow capillary refill, trophic changes and a positive Buerger's test. The weaker left femoral pulse with a bruit points to inflow (iliac or common femoral) disease as well, so his disease is multilevel, which matters when planning revascularisation. The ulcer is small, deep, punched out and pale with little exudate, on a non-weight-bearing bony prominence. The ABI confirms bilateral peripheral arterial disease, worse on the left, and a toe pressure of 24 mmHg shows severe ischaemia. Rest pain or tissue loss with objectively confirmed arterial disease is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (formerly critical limb ischaemia), which carries a high risk of amputation without revascularisation.

The peripheral vascular examination

  • Preliminaries: introduce, consent, wash hands, expose to at least above the knees, lie the patient on the bed.
  • General inspection: well or unwell, pain, walking aids, gait, body habitus, and the shoes (fit, wear, inserts).
  • Vital signs: BP, heart rate and rhythm (AF as an embolic source), SpO2, temperature.
  • Inspection of the whole limb, including the soles, heels and between the toes: amputations, ulcers, colour, necrosis, venous staining, varicosities, muscle wasting, scars, hair loss, nail changes and Charcot joints.
  • Palpation: temperature with the back of the hand from hip to foot, comparing sides; capillary refill at the big toe (normal 2 seconds or less); venous filling; pitting oedema; pulses on both sides (femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis) and the abdominal aorta.
  • Buerger's test: raise the leg to 45 degrees; pallor (and the angle at which it appears, Buerger's angle) suggests ischaemia. Then hang the leg over the bed at 90 degrees; a slow dusky red or cyanotic colour (reactive hyperaemia, rubor) confirms it.
  • Ankle-brachial index: after 10 minutes lying flat, measure the brachial systolic pressure in both arms and the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial systolic pressures with the cuff just above the ankle and a handheld Doppler, and divide the higher of the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressure by the higher brachial systolic pressure. An ABI of 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease; lower values indicate more severe disease.
  • Sensation: 10 g monofilament at three plantar sites (hallux, first and fifth metatarsal heads) per the Australian guideline, or four sites; vibration with a 128 Hz fork at the hallux; proprioception, pinprick and temperature complete the neurological picture but do not replace the monofilament or vibration.
  • To complete: urine dipstick for glucose, fundoscopy and a cardiovascular examination.

Interpreting the ABI and toe pressures

Divide the higher ankle pressure in each leg by the higher of the two brachial pressures. An ABI of 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease. In diabetes and kidney disease, calcified tibial arteries can resist compression and give a falsely normal or raised ABI, so the Australian diabetes-related foot disease guideline recommends combining pedal Doppler waveforms with the ABI and toe-brachial index. A toe pressure below 30 mmHg (or TcPO2 below 25 mmHg) in a person with a foot ulcer calls for urgent vascular imaging and consideration of revascularisation, and revascularisation should also be considered when an ulcer fails to improve over 4 to 6 weeks despite good care.

Telling ulcers apart

VenousArterialNeuropathic
CauseVenous hypertension and poor skin perfusionMicro- or macrovascular arterial disease (atherosclerotic or thromboembolic)Loss of sensation, repeated minor trauma, callus formation and breakdown
SiteGaiter area (ankle to mid calf, medial malleolus)Toes, bony prominences, sides of feet, heelPressure areas, soles of the feet
EdgeSuperficial, irregularPunched out, well defined, symmetricalRegular, thick callus, superficial to deep
BaseGranulating and sloughySloughy or eschar, pale and whiteCallus, can be necrotic
SizeLargeSmallVariable
ExudateLarge amountMinimalMinimal
PainMild to moderate ache, worse on standing and at the end of the day, better with elevationVery painful; worse at night and on elevation, eased by hanging the leg down (rest pain); claudication on walkingPainless, though burning, tingling and itching can occur
ManagementMaximise venous return: elevation and graduated compression (about 30 to 40 mmHg at the ankle) once arterial disease is excluded (ABI 0.8 to 1.2; if the ABI is above 1.2 or below 0.8, specialist assessment first)Risk factor modification, no elevation or compression, pain relief, angioplasty, bypass or amputationDiabetes control, podiatry (orthotics, foot checks), early treatment of infection, vascular surgical review

In diabetes, ulcers are often neuro-ischaemic. Mr Clayton's intact sensation, pain and non-plantar site point to a purely arterial ulcer. Infection must always be looked for in a diabetic foot ulcer: spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, pus, odour, fever, and probe to bone or plain X-ray if osteomyelitis is suspected. An uninfected ulcer should not be swabbed or treated with antibiotics.

Management (eTG Cardiovascular; Australian diabetes-related foot disease guidelines)

  • Urgent vascular surgical referral for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: arterial duplex ultrasound to assess severity and map the disease, then angiographic assessment and revascularisation by balloon angioplasty or surgical bypass. Amputation is reserved for severe cases. Kidney function matters for contrast.
  • Rest, without elevating the leg and without compression, which reduce arterial inflow and may worsen the ulcer.
  • Wound care: a dressing chosen for the wound to keep a good healing environment and prevent infection, offloading (stop the tight boots, use suitable footwear), podiatry or a multidisciplinary high-risk foot service, and regular review.
  • Risk factor modification: stop smoking completely (Quitline 13 78 48, nicotine replacement or varenicline); a single antiplatelet (aspirin 100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg daily) for symptomatic peripheral arterial disease; a high-intensity statin; better diabetes control (RACGP general HbA1c target 7% or below, 53 mmol/mol), and avoid starting an SGLT2 inhibitor while there is an active ischaemic foot ulcer; and blood pressure control, aiming below 130/80 mmHg in diabetes with albuminuria: recheck the BP and, if it stays above 130/80, start an ACE inhibitor or ARB (also indicated for confirmed albuminuria).
  • Pain: regular paracetamol, with a short-term opioid if needed for night rest pain until revascularisation, as ischaemic rest pain often needs stronger analgesia. Review medicines that slow wound healing, such as steroids (he takes none).

Safety netting

Acute limb ischaemia (sudden pain, pallor, coldness, numbness, weakness) needs 000 and the ED immediately. Signs of infection or gangrene (spreading redness, swelling, pus, odour, black skin, fever) need same-day review. He should check his feet daily, keep the urgent vascular appointment, have the ulcer reviewed at least weekly, see podiatry and see his GP in 1 to 2 weeks. Arrange retinal screening (overdue, background retinopathy).

His SpO2 of 94% with a smoker's cough and a clear chest is worth following up (for example spirometry) once the leg is managed.
points: Ask about rest pain: night pain in the forefoot eased by hanging the foot down, with an ulcer, means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and needs urgent vascular referral.
Palpate all pulse levels on both sides (femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis) and the aorta, and inspect the heels, soles and between the toes.

Arterial ulcers are small, deep, punched out and pale with little exudate, on bony prominences or toes, and very painful; venous ulcers are large, shallow, sloughy and wet in the gaiter area; neuropathic ulcers are painless and plantar with callus.

An ABI of 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease, but diabetes can falsely raise it; a toe pressure below 30 mmHg with a foot ulcer calls for urgent vascular imaging and consideration of revascularisation.
Never elevate or compress an arterial ulcer, and don't swab or give antibiotics for an uninfected one.
Secondary prevention: stop smoking, a single antiplatelet (aspirin 100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg), a high-intensity statin, and diabetes and blood pressure control.
